note: Machine-readable form of the instructor answer key. This file lives OUTSIDE the training/ directory and is therefore never served as a static asset. scripts/serve_training.py reads it server-side to grade submissions. Browser-visible answers are returned only when a student explicitly requests 'Show Solution' for a single question, which flags the scenario as assisted. Session-variable values (absolute UTC timestamps, PIDs) are deliberately NOT graded, because the sample generator re-bases them on every lab session.

q7.label: The non-alerting account

q7.solution: svc_backup from 10.0.0.30: 4 failures then a success. 4 < min_failures (5), so no alert.

q8.label: Interpreting the log lines
q8.solution: "Invalid user admin" means the account does not exist, so sshd rejected it before a password check. Combined with "Failed password for root", the attacker was cycling a username list - credential stuffing, not one targeted account.
q8.review_prompt: Does your answer explain that the account did not exist, and that the attacker was cycling a list of usernames?

q9.label: Final security finding
q9.solution: An external host (203.0.113.45) ran an automated credential attack against SSH on web-01, attempting 10 authentications across root and admin inside 2 min 12 s. Every attempt was rejected and the perimeter firewall blocked the follow-on connections, so no account was compromised.
q9.review_prompt: Does your finding name the activity, target, origin, volume, window, outcome and impact?

scenario-4.title: Linux Privilege Escalation and Reverse Shell

q1.label: Host, user and source IP

parts.label: host web-01
parts.hint: The other post-login alert is on app-01 - this one is on the Linux web server.

parts.label: user deploy
parts.hint: The user field on the web-01 post-login alert.

parts.label: source IP
parts.hint: The src_ip field of that alert.

q1.solution: host web-01, user deploy, source IP 198.51.100.77

q2.label: Logon and sudo timestamps
q2.solution: SSH logon then the sudo command 45 s later. Absolute times shift every session, so they are not graded.
q2.review_prompt: Give both @timestamp values, the logon event first.

q3.label: Elapsed gap

parts.label: elapsed time between logon and sudo
parts.hint: Subtract the logon @timestamp from the privilege_escalation @timestamp.

q3.solution: 45 seconds between the SSH logon and the sudo command

q4.label: The sudo command line

parts.label: interactive shell requested
parts.hint: Read the COMMAND= field of the sudo line in the raw_event.

parts.label: escalation target is root
parts.hint: The USER= field in the same sudo line.

q4.solution: sudo: deploy : TTY=pts/0 ; PWD=/home/deploy ; USER=root ; COMMAND=/bin/bash -i

q5.label: What the escalation achieves

parts.label: deploy became root
parts.hint: Compare the user on the logon event with the USER= field of the sudo line.

q5.solution: deploy -> root, i.e. full administrative privilege on web-01

q6.label: Why an interactive shell is dangerous
q6.solution: -i makes the shell interactive, so it presents a prompt and reads commands from the attacker. Over an established SSH session this is the standard way to retain interactive control and survive a dropped connection - the classic reverse-shell pattern.
q6.review_prompt: Does your answer explain what -i changes and why a service restart never needs it?

q7.label: The benign sudo comparison

parts.label: who ran the routine sudo commands
parts.hint: Filter privilege_escalation events on the same host and look for the lower-severity ones.

parts.label: the first routine command
parts.hint: Read process.command_line on the medium-severity events.

parts.label: the second routine command
parts.hint: The other medium-severity command line on the same host.

q7.solution: carol ran /usr/bin/systemctl restart nginx and /usr/bin/apt-get update, both recorded as privilege_escalation with severity medium.

q8.label: Fields that distinguish benign from malicious sudo

parts.label: the field holding the full command text
parts.hint: Look at the SIEM schema table on the How to Investigate page for the field that stores the complete command, not just the process name.

parts.label: the field recording how serious the event is
parts.hint: Both sudo events have the same event_type. Something else tells you one was routine and one was not - find the field that ranks it.

parts.label: the field holding the original log line
parts.hint: One field preserves the untouched source line, including the session and command markers. Use it to tell the two apart.

q8.solution: process.command_line (interactive shell vs administrative command), severity (high vs medium), and raw_event (the TTY=pts/0 / COMMAND= content).

q9.label: Final security finding
q9.solution: The deployment account deploy escalated to root on web-01, 45 s after authenticating from 198.51.100.77, requesting an interactive shell (/bin/bash -i). Unlike carol's routine systemctl and apt-get sudo activity on the same host, an interactive root shell grants complete control of the production web server.
q9.review_prompt: Does your finding contrast the malicious sudo with the benign sudo on the same host?

q10.label: SOC handover summary
q10.solution: A coordinated burst hit the estate between the first attacker event and the last firewall block. Two external addresses brute-forced SSH on web-01; 203.0.113.66 succeeded and obtained an interactive session as alice - confirmed compromise, critical. Simultaneously two accounts showed post-login hands-on-keyboard activity on app-01 and web-01. Block both external addresses, disable alice, and preserve app-01 and web-01 for forensics.
q10.review_prompt: Does your handover state the timeline, the confirmed compromise, the parallel activity and the recommended next actions?
